transcript.speech: There's a law in tech that says you can never actually get rid of inherent complexity. You can only decide who suffers from it: the person building the app, or the person using it.
This is part 16 of my Build for Good UX series, and today we're talking about Tesler's Law.
This law came from a man named Larry Tesler in the 1980s, who you can thank for inventing copy-paste, something that you probably use every day.
He was obsessed with making software as simple as possible for users.

At one point he even said, 'If a million users each waste a minute on a complexity that an engineer could have solved within a week's time, you are penalizing the user to make the engineer's job easier.'
And you? Yes, you watching this, use the internet for a ton of things that seem simple on the surface,
or clicking the Skip Intro button on Netflix,
because someone had to figure out the exact second that the intro starts and ends for thousands of shows and movies,
or Apple Pay and Face ID, where you just buy something with one tap.
You don't have to enter a password and then pull out your credit card and then enter those numbers.
There are so many more examples of this.
And the takeaway is, as much as possible, you want to take the burden and the complexity off the user and put it on yourself during the design and the development phases.
And remember that you're not building for the most perfectly patient, rational user.
Real people are busy and distracted, they just want the easiest path that'll make your product more likable.
So it's on you to handle the hard part for them. Go ahead and follow me for part 17.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Every system has an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be removed, only transferred. Designers and engineers should absorb this complexity during production rather than forcing end users to deal with it.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Demonstrations of Google search autocomplete (00:35), Netflix 'Skip Intro' button (00:37), and 1-tap Apple Pay with Face ID (00:44-00:48).
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Forcing users to perform tedious, repetitive, or complex tasks (e.g., manually skipping intros, typing full search terms, or manually entering credit card and password details).
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Handle complexity behind the scenes through automated timestamping, autocomplete predictions, and biometric authentication.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Provide 1-tap authentication (Face ID), instant intro skip overlays, and predictive search menus.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Users are busy, distracted, and prefer the easiest path; spending engineering effort to absorb complexity once prevents millions of users from wasting time and makes the product more likable.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Software development, UX/UI design, e-commerce checkout flows, search components, video streaming player controls.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The creator explains Tesler's Law (Law of Conservation of Complexity). While shifting inherent complexity to the development side improves end-user satisfaction, it requires higher development effort, automated backend data processing (such as cataloging timestamps), and integration across hardware/software systems.
inferences_not_shown_or_said: The video does not discuss operational costs or engineering tradeoffs involved in implementing automated feature sets like facial recognition algorithms or manual/algorithmic timestamp creation for video catalogs.
